title: Sustainability and Carbon Accounting
answer: Emissions data, claims checking, combined reporting, disclosure drafting and carbon credit records.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Collecting Emissions Data
children.blurb: Collecting emissions data covers the activity and factor data needed to calculate greenhouse gas emissions across an organization's chosen boundary.

children.name: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
children.blurb: Checking claims against the ledger is the practice of testing sustainability and carbon statements, such as emissions totals, renewable energy use, or credit retirements, against the underlying accounting records that support them.

children.name: Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data
children.blurb: Combining financial and non-financial data in sustainability and carbon accounting means linking monetary figures from ledgers, invoices, and asset registers with physical and qualitative measures such as emissions, energy use, water, waste, labour conditions, and governance indicators.

children.name: Drafting Sustainability Disclosures
children.blurb: Drafting sustainability disclosures is the work of preparing an organization's public statements about its environmental and social performance, most often with a heavy emphasis on greenhouse gas emissions and climate risk.

children.name: Carbon Credit Records
children.blurb: Carbon credit records are the structured documentation of verified emissions reductions or removals, including issuance, ownership, transfer, retirement, and any associated project data.

sections.body: Sustainability and carbon accounting is the work of measuring, verifying and reporting greenhouse gas emissions and related claims. Artificial intelligence is now used to pull activity data from utility bills, invoices, meter readings, travel systems and sensor feeds. It classifies spend, matches records to emissions factors and flags entries that look incomplete or inconsistent. It also helps reconcile sustainability claims against the underlying ledger and drafts first versions of disclosure text. The aim is not to replace accountants or sustainability teams but to reduce manual extraction and make large data sets easier to review. In practice, AI is a pattern finder and a drafting aid, not a source of truth.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is furthest along in data extraction, anomaly detection and first pass reconciliation. Those tasks are repetitive, rule bound and well suited to machine learning when source documents are digital and emissions factors are stable. The unsolved parts are familiar to anyone who has prepared a sustainability report. Supplier data arrives late or not at all, scopes are defined differently across jurisdictions, estimates rest on assumptions and assurance providers still need a clear audit trail. Carbon credit records add another layer because a credit's quality, ownership and retirement status can be hard to confirm from documents alone. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages show how much of this work is shaped by disclosure rules, and AI can speed up preparation without verifying what happened in the physical world or guaranteeing that a disclosure is correct.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section follow the flow of a reporting cycle. Collecting Emissions Data is the starting point, where AI helps gather and structure activity data from many sources. Checking Claims Against the Ledger is the control step, where reported figures are tested against financial and operational records. Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data is the integration step, where emissions numbers sit beside revenue, spend and other accounting measures. Drafting Sustainability Disclosures is the writing step, where AI can assemble narrative and tables for human review. Carbon Credit Records is the offset step, where credits are tracked, matched and retired, and a reader would go to each page for the specific task named in its title.
